Each center is not a wheel of light or a pastel sticker on a studio wall. It is an isolated execution environment with its own process tree, memory allocation, and I/O interfaces. concretechanges.before: This triad is not decorative. It is structural.
concretechanges.after: The triad organizes this reading; it does not establish a physiological architecture.

concretechanges.before: This is not emotional baggage. This is a buffer overflow with physiological consequences. Cortisol leaks into the relational processing queue. Oxytocin signaling gets deprioritized. The scheduler is corrupted.
concretechanges.after: “Buffer overflow” gives the overlap an image. It does not identify a cortisol leak, an oxytocin queue or a measurable scheduler failure.
The comparison suggests questions rather than diagnoses.

concretechanges.before: The symptom is the system telling you exactly where the isolation failed. Pain is not an error to suppress. Pain is the error message.
concretechanges.after: That invented log entry cannot locate a symptom’s cause. Pain deserves attention on its own terms; the image is useful only if it helps us ask what happened without pretending to diagnose it.

concretechanges.before: Attention is zero-sum. The Linux kernel's Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) will eventually allocate CPU time to every process, but without `cpu.cfs_quota_us`, one greedy process starves the others indefinitely. Your nervous system operates under the same constraint.
concretechanges.after: Attention has limits, but a Linux scheduler is only a comparison. Resource quotas can help describe the problem of one demand crowding out others; the analogy does not establish that nervous-system attention follows CFS scheduling.

concretechanges.before: This is not a hierarchy of virtue. It is a dependency graph.
concretechanges.after: I use a dependency graph here to ask what support an activity needs; this is not a verified hierarchy of human capacities.
